original_question: If G is a subcubic bipartite graph with no 4-cycle, must its strong edge-chromatic number satisfy chi_s(G) <= 7?
target_in_paper: Section 6, Open Problem 9 (restating Conjecture 31(e) from Section 4.2).
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's intended open problem almost verbatim: it has the correct graph class (subcubic, bipartite, and with no 4-cycle), the correct parameter (the strong edge-chromatic number χ_s(G)), and the correct target bound 7.
missing_details: State explicitly that 'subcubic' means maximum degree at most 3, i.e. Δ(G) ≤ 3.

Define χ_s(G): it is the minimum number of colors in a strong edge-coloring of G; equivalently, an edge-coloring in which any two edges at distance at most 2 receive distinct colors, or a proper coloring of the square of the line graph L(G)^2.
Use an explicit universal formulation such as 'every' or 'for all' to make the conjecture fully stand-alone.
If you want to mirror the paper's placement precisely, note that the statement appears first as Conjecture 31(e) in Section 4.2 and then as the stand-alone Open Problem 9 in Section 6.
refined_question: Is it true that every bipartite graph G with maximum degree at most 3 and no 4-cycles satisfies χ_s(G) ≤ 7, where χ_s(G) denotes the minimum number of colors in a strong edge-coloring of G (equivalently, an edge-coloring in which every two edges at distance at most 2 receive distinct colors)?
justification: The draft is already aimed at the right problem. The paper first presents this question in Section 4.2 as part (e) of Conjecture 31, within a six-part program for the maximum-degree-3 case, and then restates it in self-contained form in Section 6 as Open Problem 9. I kept the bipartite C4-free formulation, rather than replacing it by the broader Conjecture 32(c), because Section 4.2 explicitly says Conjecture 32(c) strengthens Conjecture 31(e), so it is a different and strictly broader target. I only added the hidden definitional material needed to make the question stand alone. The paper also indicates that 7 is the natural sharp target here by pointing to the Heawood graph as the motivating lower-bound example for part (e).
